ptsd_010 eng This is hard to write about but I’ll try to be thorough. I was 22 at the time, in my last year of university. I’d taken LSD maybe six or seven times before and always had good experiences, usually with friends in a park or at home with music. This time I decided to take a higher dose alone, because I had been reading about people having profound spiritual experiences at higher doses and I wanted that. I took what I believed to be 400ug in my room on a Saturday afternoon.

For the first two hours it was intense but manageable. Strong visuals, a lot of emotion, I cried about my grandmother who died the year before. Then around the peak, something shifted. I started to have thoughts that felt like they were coming from outside me. Messages. I became convinced that I had been chosen to understand the secret structure of reality, and that everything in my life had been arranged to lead me to this moment. The numbers on my alarm clock meant something, the pattern of the curtains meant something, the songs on the radio were speaking directly to me. At first this felt amazing, like enlightenment.

Then it turned. I realised (in the trip logic) that if I was the one who understood, I was also responsible. That the fate of everyone depended on me making the right decisions in the next few minutes. I started to feel that the world would end if I made a mistake. I couldn’t figure out what the right decision was. Every choice seemed to lead to catastrophe. I was pacing around my room, opening and closing the window, turning the lights on and off, trying to find the correct sequence. I was sobbing and talking to myself.

My flatmate came home around 9pm and found me sitting naked in the bathtub with the water running cold, repeating that I had to stay still or everyone would die. He tried to talk to me but I thought he was a test, and that if I responded wrongly it would be over. He called an ambulance.

I don’t remember the ambulance ride clearly. At the hospital they gave me a sedative. I slept for a long time. When I woke up the next day I was still not right. The acid had worn off but the thoughts hadn’t. I still felt the messages, still felt chosen and responsible. The doctors said it was a drug-induced psychosis. I was kept for observation for five days and then transferred to a psychiatric ward for another two weeks. During that time I was very confused, sometimes I knew it was the drug, sometimes I was sure it was real and they were keeping me from my mission. I was terrified of the other patients and of the nurses. My parents came from another city and I didn’t trust them either at first.

The acute LSD part was maybe 10 hours, but the experience that I’d call traumatic lasted around three weeks, and the worst part was not knowing if I’d ever be normal again. 		3 1 3 2 1 3 3 0

ptsd_013 eng My boyfriend at the time and I decided to do mushrooms together at home, around 2.5g each. He had also bought some ketamine and suggested we add a little bit at the peak to ‘deepen’ it. I’d never done ketamine and I was nervous but went along with it. The mushrooms came on strong and it was nice for a while, we were lying on the floor listening to music. Then he gave me a bump of ketamine, I don’t know how much.

Within a few minutes I couldn’t feel my body anymore. I tried to lift my hand and nothing happened. The room started to stretch and pull away, like I was falling backwards down a very long tunnel. I could hear the music but it was coming from very far away and getting slower. I tried to say his name and I couldn’t. I was completely trapped inside my head, and I became convinced I’d had a stroke and was paralysed forever. Then even that thought dissolved and there was just this grey, buzzing nothing.

When I started to come back, maybe 30-40 minutes later, I could see again, but I couldn’t move properly. He wasn’t in the room. I heard him in the kitchen on the phone, laughing. I called out and he came in and said I was ‘tripping balls’ and that it looked funny. Then he went back to the kitchen. I was lying there alone, half-paralysed, still on mushrooms, feeling completely abandoned and terrified. I crawled to the bathroom and locked the door and sat in the dark for hours. Every time he knocked I felt afraid of him, which I’d never felt before. I thought he had done this to me on purpose. The rest of the night is a blur. I remember thinking I would never trust anyone again. 		3 3 3 0 3 3 3 0

ptsd_016 eng I want to start by saying that I was experienced with psychedelics, I’d done mushrooms maybe 15 times, and I thought I knew what I was doing. That arrogance is part of the story.

It was October and I decided to go on a solo hike in a national park and take a large dose of mushrooms, around 5 grams, at a spot I’d been to before, a viewpoint about two hours’ walk from the car park. My plan was to sit there for the peak and walk back in the afternoon. I told nobody where I was going. My father had died that summer and I wanted to ‘connect’ with him and with nature.

I took the mushrooms around 11am. The come-up was very fast and strong. Within 40 minutes I couldn’t stand properly. The landscape started to breathe and pulse, and the trees looked like they were made of light. For a while it was overwhelming but beautiful. Then I saw my father. Not like a hallucination exactly, but I knew he was there, sitting on a rock nearby. He looked sick, the way he looked in the hospital at the end. He didn’t say anything. He just looked at me with this terrible sadness. I started to cry and I tried to go to him and I fell down a small slope and hurt my ankle.

After that, everything turned. The light was going (I didn’t realise how late it was, I’d lost all sense of time), and the trees around me became threatening. I heard voices in the wind, and I felt that the forest was angry that I was there. I started to believe I was going to die there, that my father had come to take me with him. Then I lost the sense of being a person at all. I was just fear, spread across the whole forest. I don’t know how long this lasted.

When I became somewhat aware again it was dark. I was cold, my ankle was swollen and I was still tripping. My phone had almost no battery and no signal. I tried to walk back but I couldn’t find the trail. I kept hearing things moving in the bushes, and every shadow looked like a figure. I sat down under a tree and wrapped myself in my rain jacket and shook all night. I was convinced I would freeze to death, and part of me thought I deserved it for not being there more for my dad.

At first light I started walking and eventually found a forest road. A ranger in a truck picked me up around 9am. I was hypothermic and had a sprained ankle, and I spent a night in a small hospital. The doctors were kind, but I was too ashamed to tell them about the mushrooms at first. When I finally told my sister what had happened, she cried and said she could have lost two family members in one year. 		3 3 3 2 3 3 1 0

ptsd_027 eng Some context first. I’m a veteran, two deployments to Afghanistan, and I was diagnosed with PTSD after I got out. I’d heard about MDMA and psilocybin trials for veterans and I was on a waiting list for one, but the wait was over a year and I was in a bad place. A buddy from my unit knew a guy who did underground sessions and I decided to go.

The guy who ran it seemed okay at first. He had a room set up in his basement with a mattress, blankets, candles, and a speaker. He said he’d been trained by people who’d worked on the trials. In the intake he asked me about my trauma and I told him the basics. We did MDMA first and then about 90 minutes later a dose of mushrooms. He said this combination would ‘open the heart and then open the mind’.

The MDMA part was actually good. For the first time in years I felt safe and warm, and I talked about some of the things I’d seen over there. I cried, he listened. Then the mushrooms kicked in and it all went sideways.

The candles turned into muzzle flashes. The speaker was playing some kind of tribal drumming and it sounded exactly like rounds hitting the vehicle. I was back in the ambush. I mean really back, not remembering it, being there. I could smell the dust and the burning rubber and I could hear my guys yelling. I saw my friend who died that day, and he was looking right at me, and his face was the way it was when we pulled him out. I knew we were taking fire from the left. I tried to get to cover.

I don’t remember everything after that. The guy running it told me later that I flipped the mattress over and got behind it and started yelling commands, and when he came close to calm me down I grabbed him and threw him into the wall. He hit his head and was bleeding. I don’t remember doing that. What I remember is that at some point I wasn’t in Afghanistan anymore but I wasn’t in the basement either. I was nowhere, there was no me, no body, no time, just pieces of memory flying around like shrapnel. I didn’t know which parts were me. I felt like I was being torn apart and every piece was screaming.

When I came back a bit, I was sitting in the corner and the guy was on the phone. I heard him say he didn’t know what to do. I thought he was calling in an airstrike on my position. I got up and ran out of the house. It was night, raining, and I ran through the neighbourhood barefoot until I found a park and hid under a slide. I don’t know how long I was there. Someone saw me and called the police. When they arrived with their lights I thought it was the enemy and I tried to fight them too. They tased me. I remember the pain and then the ground.

I spent the night in a holding cell and was taken to a VA hospital the next morning. I was still not right. I didn’t know what had happened to the guy in the basement and I was terrified I’d killed him. It turned out he had a concussion and a cut on his head. He didn’t press charges, I think because he didn’t want anyone to know what he was doing. I was charged with resisting arrest, which was later dropped after my lawyer explained my PTSD.

The whole thing lasted maybe 7 or 8 hours. The worst part, beyond all of it, was that I had hurt someone. That’s the thing I was most afraid of since coming home, that I’d lose control and hurt someone, and it happened. 		3 2 3 3 2 3 3 0

ptsd_042 eng I went to a licensed psilocybin service center, which I chose specifically because I wanted it to be safe and legal. I had a preparation session with a facilitator, a calm older woman, and she was great. I wanted to work on a general sense of anxiety that I’ve had my whole life. I took a high dose, 35mg of psilocybin, in a comfortable room with music.

The first hour was wonderful. Colours, music that felt like it was inside me, a deep sense of relaxation. I remember thinking ‘this is going to be easy’.

Then, without any warning, I couldn’t breathe. It felt like there was water in my lungs. I sat up and gasped and the facilitator came over. I tried to tell her I was drowning and I couldn’t get the words out. And then I was underwater. Not imagining it, being there. I was a small child, maybe three or four, and I was at the bottom of a pool looking up at the light and the shadows of people on the surface. I was kicking and nobody came. I swallowed water. My chest was burning. I knew I was going to die.

I’ve since learned from my mother that I nearly drowned in a hotel pool when I was three and that my uncle pulled me out. I had no conscious memory of this at all. Nobody in my family had ever mentioned it.

In the session room I apparently was gasping and clawing at my throat. The facilitator stayed calm and kept talking to me, but at some point she was worried enough about my breathing that she called the on-site supervisor, who checked my oxygen with a finger monitor. It was normal, 98 percent. They told me that. It didn’t matter. In my body I was drowning and it went on and on.

Then the drowning turned into something else. I was no longer a child, I was no longer anyone. The water became a huge dark space and I was dissolving into it. It felt like the end of me, and I fought it with everything I had. The more I fought, the worse it got. The facilitator kept saying ‘let it move through you’, and eventually, because I had no strength left, I stopped fighting. And for a moment there was a strange quiet, like floating. That moment was peaceful. But then the panic came back in waves for the rest of the session, maybe another two hours. Each wave I was underwater again.

By the end I was lying on the floor wrapped in a blanket, completely exhausted, my throat raw from gasping. The facilitator sat with me until I could walk. My partner picked me up. I didn’t speak in the car. At home I took a shower and had a panic attack when the water hit my face.

I want to say that the facilitators did everything right. This wasn’t their fault. But it was the most frightening thing I’ve ever been through. 		3 3 3 2 3 3 1 1

ptsd_049 eng I was 16 and my older cousin, who was 20, gave me LSD at a family barbecue at his parents’ place. He said it would be fun and that he’d look after me. I’d never taken anything before except a bit of weed. For the first hour I felt giggly and the colours were nice. Then my aunt called everyone to the table and I had to sit there with the whole family, my parents, my grandparents, my little sister. The food started to move on the plate. The meat looked alive. My grandfather’s face kept changing, sometimes old, sometimes young, sometimes like a skull. I couldn’t follow the conversation, people were asking me questions about school and I didn’t know how to answer.

I became terrified that my parents would find out. Then I became terrified that I’d broken my brain and would be like this forever, and that my life was over at 16. I went to the bathroom and locked the door and looked in the mirror and didn’t recognise my own face. My cousin came and knocked and told me to come out and act normal. He sounded annoyed, not worried. I didn’t come out for an hour. My mum knocked and asked if I was sick and I said I had a stomach ache.

We went home and I lay in my bed all night with my eyes open, watching the ceiling crawl, sure that I was going insane. I had school the next morning and I went because I was afraid that staying home would make my parents suspicious. I sat through classes still feeling strange, everything too loud and too bright. I didn’t tell anyone for years. 		3 1 3 1 1 3 3 0

ptsd_051 eng I booked a five-day ‘transformational’ retreat in the Netherlands that combined daily breathwork sessions with three truffle ceremonies. I was in a stable place in my life and I went mostly out of curiosity and for personal growth. Looking back, the schedule was intense: up at 6am for cold plunges and breathwork, ceremony every other day, very little sleep, a lot of sharing circles in the evenings that went until midnight.

The first ceremony was beautiful. I felt a lot of love, cried about my grandmother, and felt connected to the group. The facilitators praised me in the sharing circle for being ‘so open’.

The second ceremony was two days later, after two nights of maybe four hours of sleep. They gave a higher dose. This time I went somewhere very big. I felt that I was receiving messages about my purpose. I understood that I had a special role to play, that I had been chosen to bring a new kind of consciousness into the world. I felt incredibly powerful and also very responsible. When I came out of the ceremony, the feeling didn’t go away. I couldn’t sleep that night at all. My thoughts were racing. I felt I could see connections between everything, people’s names, the patterns on the wallpaper, the timing of birdsong. I wrote pages and pages in my notebook.

The next day in the breathwork session I hyperventilated, as instructed, and I went into a state where I was laughing and crying at the same time and shouting. The facilitators said this was a breakthrough. I told the group in the circle that evening that I was a vessel for a higher intelligence and that I knew things about each of them. I think I said some quite intrusive things to people. Some of them looked frightened. One of the facilitators took me aside and said that maybe I should skip the third ceremony. I was furious, I thought they were jealous of my awakening.

That night I didn’t sleep again. I walked around the grounds in the dark, talking to the trees. I was convinced that the stars were sending me signals. Around 4am I knocked on the facilitators’ door to tell them I’d understood the secret of time. They looked very worried.

In the morning they told me that it was best for me to leave the retreat. They didn’t call a doctor. They drove me to the train station and gave me back part of my money. I don’t think they wanted any trouble. I had to travel home alone, by train and plane, in what I now know was a manic state. At the airport I was talking to strangers about my mission, I missed my flight because I got lost in the duty-free looking for ‘signs’, and I was crying and laughing in the bathroom. A security officer noticed me and called a medic, who asked me some questions and then let me go when I calmed down for a moment. I eventually got a later flight.

When I arrived home my partner picked me up and immediately knew something was very wrong. She took me to the emergency room the next day. I didn’t think I needed help; I thought I was enlightened. It took a few days before I could see that something was not right with my mind. The crash came about a week later. 		1 2 3 2 1 3 3 0

I kept walking from room to room, trying not to wake my parents. When the sun finally came up I cried from relief. 3 1 3 0 0 2 1 1

ptsd_055 eng I took a high dose of 1P-LSD, maybe 250-300ug, by myself on a Saturday and decided to walk around the city because I thought it would be interesting. For a while it was. I got on a train just to get away and rode it to the end of the line.

When I got out I was in a part of the city I didn’t know at all. My phone battery was dead. It was getting dark. I was walking around for hours, trying to find my way back, and every street looked the same. I was crying and talking to myself. People were crossing the street to avoid me. At one point I sat down on a bench and a homeless man sat next to me and asked if I was alright. I told him that everyone was robots and he laughed in a kind way and said ‘yeah, sometimes it feels like that’. He stayed with me for a long time and shared his tea from a thermos. He told me about his life. Eventually he walked me to a bus stop and told me which bus to take. I don’t know his name. I think about him a lot. 		3 0 3 1 0 3 3 1

I had no idea what had happened and thought I’d died and come back. 3 1 2 0 3 2 2 0
ptsd_057 ger Ich hatte bei Freunden Pilze genommen. Irgendwann war ich überzeugt, dass alle meine Gedanken laut hörbar sind und dass alle wissen, was ich denke. Ich habe mich furchtbar geschämt und mich in eine Ecke gesetzt. 3 0 2 0 0 1 2 0
ptsd_058 eng This happened about three years ago. I’m going to describe it in detail because I think the details matter.

Three friends and I rented a cabin in the mountains for a long weekend. Two of us, me and my friend J, had experience with LSD. The other two had only done mushrooms once. We planned to take LSD on Saturday, with one person staying sober, but on the day everyone wanted to take it, and the sober-sitter idea was abandoned. In hindsight that was the first mistake. We each took about 200ug around 2pm.

The afternoon was great. We hiked down to the lake, lay on the rocks, watched the clouds. The two less-experienced friends were giggling and having a great time. J was quieter than usual, but I didn’t think much of it. I was having a beautiful trip, feeling very connected to nature.

Around sunset, things started to change with J. He began saying that he could hear the lake speaking to him. At first we thought he was joking. Then he started saying that the lake wanted him, that he had to go to it. He was staring at the water and wouldn’t respond to us. His eyes looked completely different, like there was nobody behind them. I tried to talk to him and he suddenly pushed me away, hard, and shouted that I was one of ‘them’. I didn’t know who ‘them’ was.

I was still very high, and his behaviour sent my own trip into a nightmare. The sunset turned blood red. The trees around the lake looked like they were leaning in to watch. I felt that something evil had come for J and that it would come for me next. The other two were panicking and crying. One of them said we should call for help, but there was no signal at the lake.

J then walked straight into the lake with his clothes on. It was early autumn and the water was freezing. He kept walking until he was up to his chest, and then he started swimming out towards the middle. I don’t really know how I made the decision, but I went in after him. The cold hit me like a wall. On LSD it felt like I was being stabbed with a thousand knives, and I felt my body dissolving into the black water. I lost the sense of where I ended and the lake began. For a moment I genuinely didn’t know if I was alive. I remember thinking very clearly: this is how I die.

Somehow I reached him. He was thrashing and shouting, and he hit me in the face. I grabbed his jacket and started pulling him back. I don’t know how long it took. It felt like hours. When we got to the shore, the other two pulled us out. J was shaking and blue-lipped and kept mumbling about the voice in the water. I couldn’t stop shaking either. One of the others ran up to the cabin to find signal and call emergency services.

Waiting for them was the worst part. It was dark by then. We wrapped J in every blanket and jacket we had. He alternated between staring blankly and screaming that we were trying to kill him. At one point he tried to run back to the water and we had to hold him down. Holding a friend down while he screams at you, while you’re on LSD and the world is melting, is something I will never forget. I felt like a monster. I felt like I was in a horror film. I was also convinced, part of the time, that maybe he was right, maybe we were the bad guys and I just didn’t know it.

The mountain rescue arrived after about an hour and a half with a police car and an ambulance. The lights and the uniforms made everything worse. They separated us and asked us questions. I couldn’t make sense of their words. They took J away in the ambulance, sedated. They checked me for hypothermia and let me stay at the cabin with the others, but a police officer stayed with us for a while and took our details. I kept asking if J would be okay and nobody could tell me.

The rest of the night, the three of us sat in the cabin with all the lights on. Nobody slept. The LSD was still going and every sound outside sounded like footsteps. I kept seeing J’s face, his empty eyes. I kept feeling the cold water closing over my head. I felt that something had broken in the world.

J was in a psychiatric ward for three weeks. He had a psychotic episode that lasted well beyond the trip. He’s mostly okay now, but our friendship has never been the same. He doesn’t remember most of that night, and I remember all of it. 		3 3 3 3 3 3 3 0

The kambo made me vomit and my face swelled up and I felt like I was suffocating. My heart was racing and I lay on the ground for an hour unable to move. I was still weak in the evening but they said the ceremony would ‘complete the cleansing’. The ayahuasca hit me very hard because I was dehydrated and exhausted. I saw myself as a corpse being eaten by insects. I couldn’t get up to go to the toilet and soiled myself. I felt utterly humiliated and terrified. Nobody came to help me until morning. 3 1 3 3 3 3 2 0

Dort hat uns jemand Pilz-Shakes verkauft, und ich habe einen ganzen getrunken, ohne zu wissen, wie stark er ist. Nach einer Stunde war ich völlig weg. Die Musik, die Feuer-Shows, die tausend Menschen am Strand, alles hat sich zu einem Albtraum vermischt. Ich habe meine Freundin verloren und bin am Strand umhergeirrt. Irgendwann habe ich bemerkt, dass meine Tasche weg war, mit Pass, Geld und Handy. Ich hatte panische Angst, nie wieder nach Hause zu kommen. Dann kamen zwei Männer in Uniform, ich weiß nicht, ob es echte Polizisten waren, und haben mich gefragt, ob ich Drogen genommen habe. Sie haben gedroht, mich ins Gefängnis zu bringen, wenn ich nicht bezahle. Ich hatte kein Geld. Sie haben mich eine Weile festgehalten und angeschrien, bis sie mich irgendwann gehen ließen. Ich habe bis zum Morgen hinter einem Boot gesessen und gezittert. Meine Freundin hat mich am nächsten Tag gefunden. 3 0 3 0 0 3 3 0

ptsd_061 eng My roommate and I took mushrooms in our student flat on a Friday night. Neither of us had much experience. We’d each eaten about 2.5g. For the first hour we were laughing a lot. Then he went quiet and said he felt like his heart was doing something weird. I looked at him and his face started to look grey and sick, and I got scared that he was having a heart attack. He saw that I was scared, and that made him more scared. Within minutes we were both in full panic, feeding off each other. He was pacing up and down saying ‘I’m dying, I’m dying’, and I was sitting on the floor convinced that I was going to have to watch my best friend die and that it would be my fault because I bought the mushrooms.

Then my own body started doing things. My hands went numb and tingly, my chest got tight, and I thought maybe the mushrooms were poisonous and we were both dying. I looked up poisonous mushrooms on my phone and the pictures made everything worse. The walls were breathing and the light from the phone screen was burning my eyes.

I called my mum. It was 1am. I was crying and I told her we’d taken mushrooms and were dying. She stayed calm somehow, and told me to put my roommate on the phone too, and she talked to us both for over an hour, telling us to breathe, asking us silly questions about what we could see. She said if anything got worse she would call an ambulance, and she checked on us every ten minutes after we hung up. My dad drove three hours that night to come get me. I was so ashamed when he arrived. He didn’t say much, he just made us toast and tea and sat with us until morning. 		3 0 2 0 3 2 3 1

Ich war völlig überfordert, alles war laut, dunkel und eng, und ich fand den Ausgang nicht. Fremde Menschen haben mich angefasst. Ich hatte das Gefühl, in der Hölle zu sein, und konnte nicht atmen. Irgendwann hat mich ein Türsteher rausgeführt. 3 0 2 1 1 3 3 0
ptsd_063 eng I’m a mother of two. My husband and I don’t get much time to ourselves, and for our tenth anniversary we went to a cabin for the weekend and left the kids with my sister. We’d both done mushrooms a couple of times in college and decided to do it again, a moderate dose, maybe 2 grams each.

About an hour in, while we were sitting by the fire and feeling lovely, my phone rang. It was my sister. My younger son, who’s three, had a high fever and was having what she thought was a seizure. She was panicking. She said she was calling an ambulance.

I can’t describe what that did to me. I couldn’t think. The words she was saying were coming apart. I was trying to understand what was happening to my son and my mind was full of colours and shapes and the fire was crackling and it all felt like a nightmare. I kept asking her to repeat things. My husband took the phone and he was in a similar state. We couldn’t drive. We were two hours away. We were completely useless to our child, who needed us.

Then the visions started. I saw my son’s little body, blue and still. I saw a small coffin. I saw myself at a funeral, and everyone was looking at me, knowing that I had been off taking drugs while my son died. I felt that this was a punishment, that the universe was showing me what kind of mother I really was. I was on the floor of the cabin, sobbing and screaming. My husband tried to hold me but he was crying too.

My sister called again about forty minutes later from the hospital. It was a febrile seizure, which I now know is quite common and usually harmless, and my son was okay. But in that state I didn’t believe her. I thought she was lying to protect me. I kept saying ‘tell me the truth’. I asked her to put him on the phone and he was asleep, so I couldn’t hear him, and my mind filled in the worst.

The rest of the night I sat by the window waiting for the drugs to wear off so we could drive. Every minute felt like an hour. I kept seeing the coffin. We left at 6am and drove straight to the hospital. When I finally held my son, he was sleepy and cranky and completely fine, and I couldn’t stop shaking.

My sister was kind about it but I know she was shocked when we told her. I’ve never felt so much shame in my life. 		3 0 3 3 1 3 3 0

ptsd_065 ger Ich habe an einer Psilocybin-Studie für Menschen mit therapieresistenter Depression teilgenommen. Ich hatte große Hoffnungen. Die Sitzung fand in einem gemütlich eingerichteten Raum in der Klinik statt, mit zwei Begleitern. Ich bekam eine hohe Dosis.

Dann kam das Gefühl, eingesperrt zu sein. Der Raum wurde enger. Die Musik, die eigentlich beruhigend sein sollte, klang wie eine Totenmesse. Die Begleiter haben mich nicht allein gelassen, das muss ich sagen. Eine von ihnen hat meine Hand gehalten und immer wieder gesagt, dass ich sicher bin. Aber ich konnte das nicht fühlen. Das ging vielleicht drei Stunden so. Gegen Ende wurde es etwas leichter, und ich hatte einen kurzen Moment, in dem ich die Hand der Begleiterin wirklich gespürt habe, als etwas Warmes. Das war der einzige Lichtblick. 		3 1 2 1 1 3 1 1

ptsd_067 eng I took a high dose of mushrooms, about 5 grams, at home with my partner. It was my idea, I’d read about ‘heroic doses’. She took a smaller dose to look after me.

About an hour and a half in, I looked at her and something was wrong. She looked exactly like her, but I knew with absolute certainty that it wasn’t her. It was someone, or something, wearing her face. Her movements were slightly off, her voice was slightly wrong, like a recording. I tried to stay calm and test her. I asked her questions only she would know. She answered them correctly, which made it worse, because it meant the impostor had access to her memories. I started thinking that the real her was somewhere else, maybe dead, and this thing had taken her place.

I locked myself in the bedroom with our cat. The cat was the only thing I trusted. I sat in the corner holding him and listening to her knocking on the door and calling my name, and every time I heard her voice I felt sick with fear. I was also sure the thing could change shape and might come through the walls. I could see the walls bulging.

She called my brother, who came over. I didn’t trust him either. They talked to me through the door for hours. Eventually I fell asleep, or passed out, holding the cat.

The next morning I woke up and the drug had worn off, but the feeling hadn’t fully gone. I looked at her and I knew in my head it was her, but there was a tiny voice saying ‘are you sure?’. That voice lasted for days. I couldn’t kiss her. I’d test her with questions. She was very hurt and scared. My brother took me to a doctor on the third day. 		3 0 3 2 0 2 3 0

Then they turned away from me, all at once, and I felt cast out, rejected by the universe itself. I came back and immediately burst into tears. ptsd_072 eng I am a gay man from a country where homosexuality is not accepted, and where drug use is punished harshly. I’ll leave the country unnamed. At the time of this experience I was living in the capital, very much in the closet at work and with my family. My boyfriend and I had a small apartment that we said we shared as ‘friends’.

A friend who’d lived in Europe brought back some LSD and gave us two tabs. We waited for a weekend when we had nothing planned and took them at home. For a few hours it was the most beautiful experience. We felt free, we danced, we laughed, we held each other. For the first time in my life I felt completely accepted as I am.

Then, in the evening, we heard loud banging on the door. Police. Later I found out that our neighbour had heard music and two men’s voices, and had been suspicious of us for a long time. I was at the peak of the trip. The banging sounded like the end of the world. My boyfriend tried to hide the remaining tabs. I opened the door because I thought that if I didn’t, they would break it.

Four officers came in. They saw how we looked, our pupils, and they knew immediately. They searched the apartment and found the foil with the tabs. They found photos on my phone of me and my boyfriend. One of them started shouting the word they use for gay men, and hit my boyfriend in the face. I froze. The colours were still moving, the officers’ faces were melting and turning into animal faces. I didn’t know if this was real or if I had gone insane.

They handcuffed us and took us to the police station in separate cars. I sat in the back of the car and watched the city lights stream past like rivers of blood. In the station they put me in a small room with one bare bulb. The bulb was pulsing. I was alone for what felt like days. Then two officers came in and interrogated me. They wanted names: who gave us the drugs, who else was gay, who else was in our circle. When I didn’t answer, one of them slapped me repeatedly. They threatened to call my family and my employer. They said I would go to prison for years and that I’d be raped there. I was still tripping and I believed everything they said, more than believed, I saw it happening.

At some point I lost myself completely. There was no more me, just fear and the bulb and the voices. I think I gave them some names. I don’t remember. That’s one of the things I can’t forgive myself for.

We were held for two days. My boyfriend had a broken nose. A cousin of mine who is a lawyer got us out. I don’t know what he paid. My family found out about everything. My father didn’t speak to me for a year.

Three months later, my boyfriend and I left the country. We applied for asylum in Europe. That’s where I’m living now. 		3 3 3 2 2 3 3 0

My children grabbed me and held me back. They thought I’d lost my mind from grief, they didn’t know about the mushrooms.

Then the vision changed. The sea was full of bodies, hundreds of grey faces under the surface, all looking up. I understood that this was death, and that he was among them, and that I had thrown him there. I felt I’d killed him. I couldn’t stop sobbing.

My friend tried to calm me and told my children what was happening. My daughter was furious with her. The boat ride back took 40 minutes and I lay curled in the bottom of the boat with my eyes shut, but the faces were there behind my eyelids too. When we reached the harbour I couldn’t stand up. ptsd_109 eng I took LSD with two friends at a cabin by a lake. ptsd_118 eng I want to describe this carefully because I’ve never read about anyone having exactly this experience.

I booked a ‘dark retreat’: seven days in total darkness in a small hut in the mountains, with food passed in through a light-tight hatch. The idea, according to the organisers, is that after a few days in the dark the brain begins to produce its own psychedelic states. On top of that, they offered an optional ‘plant medicine’ on day four, which turned out to be a brew containing harmala alkaloids and DMT-containing bark, an ayahuasca analogue. I’d done ayahuasca twice before with good experiences and I wanted to go deeper. I signed the waiver.

Days one to three were hard but manageable. I lost track of time quickly. I slept and woke at random. I meditated. I began to see coloured lights and shapes, which the organiser said was normal. By day three I was having vivid waking dreams. I heard voices sometimes, mostly my own thoughts, but very loud. I was lonely but also curious.

On day four the brew was passed through the hatch with a small candle, which I was told to blow out after drinking. I drank it and sat in the darkness.

What followed I can only describe as the darkness coming alive. Without any light, the visions had nothing to anchor to. They filled the whole space. I saw the walls of the hut covered in eyes, thousands of them, opening one by one. I heard breathing that wasn’t mine. Something sat down next to me on the mattress. I felt the mattress dip. I reached out and there was nothing there, but I felt it lean against me.

Then I lost my body. In the darkness there was no way to check where my hands were, no way to see myself. I felt I had become the darkness itself, an infinite black space, and that there was no hut, no mountain, no world. I had always existed in the dark and the light was the dream. I kept trying to remember a single image from my life, my mother’s kitchen, my partner’s face, and each time the image was swallowed as soon as it formed.

I don’t know how long this lasted. In the dark there’s no time. It could have been an hour or twelve. At some point I started screaming, and I realised that nobody could hear me. The hut was far from the main house. The protocol was that you knock three times on the hatch in an emergency. I couldn’t find the hatch. I crawled along the walls feeling for it, and the walls seemed to go on forever, corners kept appearing where there shouldn’t be corners. I was convinced I was trapped in an infinite maze in the dark, and that I’d die there.

Eventually I found the hatch and knocked. Nothing happened. I knocked again and again until my knuckles bled. I don’t know how long it took, but eventually it opened and light came in, just a sliver, and it was like being hit by lightning. The organiser’s voice asked if I wanted to end the retreat. I said yes. He said it might be better to ‘stay with the process’ until morning. I begged. He said he would come back in an hour. He closed the hatch.

That hour was the worst of my life. I sat by the hatch with my hand on it, rocking back and forth, feeling the presence next to me, hearing it breathe.

When he came back he opened the door. The light was blinding. He led me out with a blindfold, because coming into full light suddenly can be harmful, he said. I spent the rest of the day in a room with dim light, alone, still tripping. Every shadow moved. I left the next morning. 		3 3 3 3 1 3 2 0

My partner didn’t know I’d taken anything.

I said ‘okay’ because I didn’t know what else to say. I tried to sober up, splashing water on my face, which of course does nothing. When the doorbell rang, my partner handed me our daughter and left in a hurry. And then I was alone with a toddler while tripping hard.

She wanted to play. She wanted dinner. She wanted her bath. Everything she asked for was a mountain. Her face kept changing, sometimes she looked like a baby, sometimes like an old woman, sometimes her eyes were huge and black. I was terrified that I’d drop her, that I’d hurt her, that I’d forget she was there. I kept counting her fingers. When she cried because I couldn’t find her favourite cup, the crying filled the whole house and the walls pulsed with it. I felt like the worst father in the world and that this was a test I was failing.

I sat on the floor of her room with her on my lap for hours, reading the same book over and over because it was the only thing I could manage. The words on the page kept moving. My friends thought it was funny until they saw how scared I was. 3 0 1 3 1 3 1 0
ptsd_124 eng This is the first time I’ve written this down.

I was married to a man who was controlling and sometimes violent. I didn’t see it that way at the time, I thought it was normal, that he was stressed, that I provoked him. He had done mushrooms when he was younger and kept saying they would ‘open me up’ and make me less uptight. I didn’t want to, but he insisted, and saying no to him was never easy. So one Saturday when our kids were at his parents’, we both took mushrooms.

For the first hour, I felt strangely clear. It was like a fog lifted. I looked at him and saw him, really saw him. I saw the coldness in his eyes. I saw all the times he’d hurt me, one after another, like slides. I’d been telling myself stories for nine years, and the mushrooms took the stories away.

He noticed I was looking at him differently and asked what was wrong. I said something, I don’t remember exactly, something like ‘you scare me’. That set him off. He started shouting that I was ungrateful, that I was crazy, that I was ruining the trip. He got very close to my face. On the mushrooms his face became huge and red and his voice boomed like thunder. Then he grabbed my arm and pulled me off the sofa and pushed me against the wall. My head hit the wall. I saw stars, real stars and mushroom stars together.

I don’t know how I knew what to do, but I did. I went completely limp and quiet, because I knew from experience that if I fought, it would be worse. He let go and went to the kitchen to get a beer, still shouting. I sat on the floor, and in that state I had a single, very clear thought: if I stay, one day he’ll kill me. It wasn’t a hallucination. It was the clearest thought I’d ever had.

The rest of the trip was a nightmare. He calmed down after an hour and wanted to cuddle and ‘have a nice trip’, as if nothing had happened. I let him, because I was afraid. Inside, I felt my whole self cracking apart. I felt like I was two people, one lying on the sofa smiling, and one floating above, screaming. The walls were breathing, and I kept seeing the faces of my children. I lay there for hours, pretending, while my mind was howling.

Two weeks later, while he was at work, I took the kids and went to a women’s shelter. 		3 2 2 1 3 2 3 1
ptsd_125 ger Ich hatte auf LSD ein Ego-Tod-Erlebnis. Am Anfang war das sehr angsteinflößend, ich dachte, ich verliere den Verstand und sterbe. Ich habe mich verzweifelt an meinem Namen festgehalten, und er ist mir trotzdem entglitten. Dann habe ich losgelassen, und es kam ein Gefühl von großer Weite und Frieden. Danach war ich sehr erschöpft, aber auch dankbar. Es war die schwierigste und gleichzeitig die wertvollste Erfahrung meines Lebens. 3 3 2 0 0 0 0 3
ptsd_126 eng I was at a friend’s house and he offered me DMT from a vape pen. I had smoked DMT once before and it was fine. What I didn’t know was that this pen contained 5-MeO-DMT, which is a completely different substance and much stronger. I took one deep hit.

Instantly, everything disappeared. Not into visions, just into white nothingness. There was no me, no room, no world. I don’t know how to describe it except as total annihilation. In that state there was no fear, because there was no one to be afraid.

The fear came when I started coming back. I was on the floor, I didn’t know how. My body was doing things on its own, my arms and legs were jerking and I was making strange noises. I couldn’t breathe properly. It felt like my chest had forgotten how. My friend told me later that I had stopped breathing for maybe 20 or 30 seconds and that he started shaking me and was about to call an ambulance when I gasped.

For the next 20 minutes I was in total terror. I didn’t know who I was. I knew there had been nothing and that the nothing was still right there, behind everything, and that I could fall back into it any second. I clutched my friend’s arm and kept asking him if I was alive. He was pale and scared. He kept apologising. I lay on his sofa for an hour, unable to stand, and every time I closed my eyes I felt the white nothing pulling at me. 		3 3 3 0 3 2 2 0
ptsd_127 eng LSD at a concert. I became convinced that the band was singing about me, that every lyric was a message about my life and my sins. Cried through the whole set. 3 0 2 1 0 3 1 0
ptsd_128 ger Ich war im Erasmus-Semester in Spanien. An einem Wochenende bin ich mit ein paar Leuten aus dem Studentenwohnheim an die Küste gefahren, und wir haben am Strand LSD genommen. Es war meine erste Erfahrung. Am Anfang war es wunderschön, das Meer, die Sterne, das Lagerfeuer.

Irgendwann bin ich allein am Strand entlanggelaufen, weil ich das Meer sehen wollte. Ich habe mich verlaufen. Ich wusste nicht mehr, wo die anderen waren. Ich habe mein Handy aus der Tasche genommen, um sie anzurufen, und es ist mir in den Sand gefallen. Ich habe es nicht wiedergefunden. Ich hatte keine Ahnung, wie unser Hostel hieß, ich hatte nur die Adresse im Handy.

Es war Nacht, und ich war allein an einem fremden Strand in einem fremden Land und konnte kaum Spanisch. Drei Männer kamen auf mich zu und haben mich angesprochen. Ich habe nicht verstanden, was sie wollten. Einer hat mich am Arm gefasst, ein anderer hat gelacht. Ich habe mich losgerissen und bin weggerannt, barfuß, durch den Sand und dann über eine Straße. Ich weiß nicht, ob sie mir gefolgt sind. In meinem Kopf waren sie überall, hinter jedem Auto, in jedem Schatten.

Sie hat mich mit in ihr Café genommen, mir einen Kaffee gegeben und mit ihrem Handy meine Mitbewohnerin über Facebook gesucht. Ich bin ihr unendlich dankbar. 		3 0 3 1 1 3 3 0

I remember waking up in a hammock with my hands tied, because apparently I’d been wandering into the jungle. I remember not knowing what country I was in. I remember a man holding a cup to my lips. The other participants said I was talking to invisible people for hours and tried to walk into the river. 3 0 3 3 3 3 3 0

ptsd_133 eng I was in my third year of medical school when this happened. I’m writing it in detail because I’ve had to tell it so many times, to police, to the university, to my therapist, that it has become a kind of script, but I’ll try to write what it felt like rather than just what happened.

There was a party in a flat on the third floor of an old building. I’d taken LSD a handful of times before, always in calm settings. That night a friend of mine, I’ll call him M, had brought some tabs, and five or six of us took one each around 10pm. M took two. The flat had a small balcony overlooking a courtyard, with a low iron railing.

For the first two hours it was a great party. Music, dancing, a lot of laughing. I remember lying on the floor watching the ceiling lamp turn into a jellyfish and thinking how lucky I was to have these friends. M was in a very euphoric mood, talking about how he felt he could fly, but we all laughed because he always said stuff like that.

Around midnight, I went out onto the balcony to get some air. M was there, sitting on the railing with his legs dangling over the courtyard, looking at the sky. I said something like ‘mate, get down from there’. He laughed and said he wanted to touch the moon. I remember the moon looked enormous, like it was right above us, and in my state it seemed almost reasonable that he’d want to touch it. I don’t know why I didn’t grab him immediately. I’ve asked myself that question a thousand times.

He stood up on the railing. I reached out for him and my hand touched his jacket, and then he wasn’t there. There was no scream. Just a silence, and then a sound from the courtyard below, a sound I will never be able to describe and never forget.

I looked over the railing. He was lying on the cobblestones, twisted, not moving. On LSD, the courtyard was swirling, the cobblestones were moving like water, and his body looked like it was sinking into them. I screamed. People came running onto the balcony. Someone started screaming too. Someone else called an ambulance. I ran down the stairs, three floors, I don’t remember the stairs at all, and I was in the courtyard next to him.

And here is the thing that haunts me most. I’m a medical student. I knew what to do, in theory. Check airway, breathing, circulation. Don’t move his neck. But I couldn’t think. My hands were shaking and they kept changing shape. His face was bleeding and the blood was a colour I’d never seen, too bright, glowing. I could hear him breathing, a horrible gurgling sound, and I didn’t know if I was hearing it or imagining it. I knelt next to him and held his hand and said his name over and over. A neighbour came out, an older man, and he was the one who actually did something useful: he kept M’s head still and talked to the ambulance dispatcher. I just knelt there.

The ambulance and the police arrived together. The lights. Blue lights bouncing off the walls of the courtyard, turning everything into a strobe nightmare. The paramedics pushed me away, which was right. I watched them work on him. They put a collar on him and a mask and lifted him onto a stretcher. One of them asked me what he’d taken and I said LSD, and he looked at my eyes and said ‘and you too, I see’.

The police separated everyone and took our names. A young officer asked me to describe what happened. I tried. I said he wanted to touch the moon. She wrote that down with a blank face. I realised how insane it sounded. I started to believe that they’d think I pushed him. My hand had been on his jacket. Had I pushed him? In that state I genuinely didn’t know. Maybe I had. Maybe I’d reached out to grab him and actually pushed. I’ve had that doubt ever since, even though I know rationally that I didn’t.

They let us go around 3am. I didn’t know if M was alive. I walked home alone through the city, still tripping. Every streetlight looked like the moon. Every sound was that sound from the courtyard. When I got home I sat in the shower with my clothes on and stayed there until the water ran cold, and then I stayed there anyway.

At 7am, a friend texted that M was alive, in intensive care, with a broken pelvis, broken arm and a head injury. He survived. He’s mostly recovered now, with some lasting problems with his leg. He doesn’t remember anything from that night after about 11pm. 		3 1 3 2 2 3 3 0
ptsd_134 ger Wir waren zu dritt in einer Hütte im Schwarzwald und hatten Pilze gegessen. Gegen Abend ist der Strom ausgefallen, wahrscheinlich wegen eines Sturms. Wir hatten nur ein paar Kerzen. In dem flackernden Licht wurde die Hütte zu einem fremden, bedrohlichen Ort. Die Schatten an den Wänden haben sich bewegt und Gestalten gebildet. Ich hörte draußen Schritte, ganz deutlich, rund um die Hütte. Die anderen sagten, das sei der Wind, aber ich war mir sicher, dass jemand da draußen ist und uns beobachtet.

Dann ist einer meiner Freunde rausgegangen, um nach dem Sicherungskasten zu sehen, und kam nicht zurück. Fünf Minuten, zehn Minuten, zwanzig Minuten. Für mich war es eine Ewigkeit. Ich war mir sicher, dass ihn das Wesen draußen geholt hat und dass wir die Nächsten sind. Ich habe mich mit dem anderen Freund in eine Ecke gesetzt, wir haben uns aneinander geklammert. Ich habe gezittert und konnte nicht mehr klar denken. Ich habe angefangen zu beten, obwohl ich nicht gläubig bin.

Als er schließlich zurückkam, nass und lachend, weil er sich im Dunkeln verlaufen hatte, habe ich ihn angeschrien und dann geweint. Er hat nicht verstanden, warum ich so reagiere. Der Strom kam die ganze Nacht nicht zurück, und ich habe bis zum Morgengrauen mit offenen Augen dagesessen und auf die Tür gestarrt. 		3 0 2 3 1 3 2 0

ptsd_136 eng I went to a retreat in Mexico for a week of ayahuasca ceremonies. The ceremonies were held in an open-sided palapa in the jungle. On the third night, at the peak of a very strong experience, I felt a sudden burning pain in my foot, like being stabbed with a hot needle. I looked down and in the candlelight I saw a scorpion crawling away.

The pain spread up my leg. My foot went numb and then my lips started tingling. In my state I was convinced that I was dying, that the poison was moving towards my heart and that I had maybe minutes left. The visions turned into scorpions, thousands of them pouring out of the ground and over my body. I screamed. One of the facilitators came over, and when I told her, she looked at my foot and said it was probably a scorpion and that most of them in the area weren’t dangerous to adults. But she also looked worried and went to get the retreat leader.

They decided to take me to a local clinic, which was 40 minutes away on a bumpy dirt road. I lay in the back of a pickup truck, still in the middle of the ayahuasca, vomiting over the side, with my foot burning and the stars swirling overhead. I thought I was going to die in that truck. I said goodbye to my family in my head. I had visions of my mother crying at my funeral.

At the clinic the doctor gave me an injection and kept me under observation for the night. The sting turned out to be painful but not life-threatening. I lay on a hard bed in a white room under a fluorescent light, alone, still feeling the effects of the brew. A gecko on the wall kept turning into a scorpion. I didn’t sleep. The next morning I was driven back to the retreat, where everyone wanted to hear about my ‘initiation’. I left two days early. 		3 0 2 3 3 3 2 0

When it ended, eight hours later, I lay there exhausted with a bruised cheek. The course had a section called ‘integration’ which said to journal about your breakthrough. I didn’t have a breakthrough. I had the worst night of my life. 		3 1 3 3 1 3 1 0

ptsd_145 eng Two friends and I went camping on a small island off the coast that you can walk to at low tide. We took mushrooms in the afternoon, around 2.5g each, and spent hours exploring rock pools. It was beautiful, the anemones were glowing and the sea sounded like breathing.

At some point I wandered off on my own to a rocky outcrop at the far end of the island to watch the sunset. I lost track of time completely. When I looked down, the water had come in all around the rock I was sitting on. The path back was under water. In my state, the sea looked like it was rising by the second, swallowing everything. I was sure that the whole island would disappear and that I’d drown. I screamed for my friends, but the wind took my voice.

It got dark. The water was black and loud, smashing against the rocks below me. I clung to the rock with both hands. My fingers were bleeding from the barnacles. I started seeing shapes in the waves, faces, arms reaching up. I was certain they wanted to pull me in. I felt my sense of self dissolving into the roar, like I was already part of the sea.

My friends had realised I was missing and were searching with their phone torches. They found me about two hours later. The tide had started going out again by then, and they waded out to me, knee-deep. I couldn’t let go of the rock at first. They had to peel my fingers off one by one. Back at the tent I shook all night, wrapped in every sleeping bag we had. I kept hearing the waves as if they were inside the tent. 		3 2 3 2 2 3 2 0

Irgendwann bin ich auf den Boden gesackt und habe mich nur noch zusammengerollt. Ich hatte das Gefühl, dass die Kabine ein Sarg ist, in dem ich lebendig begraben bin. Ich weiß nicht, wie lange ich dort war, vielleicht zwanzig Minuten, vielleicht eine Stunde. Ein Türsteher hat schließlich die Tür von außen aufgebrochen, weil jemand gehört hatte, wie ich weine. Er hat mich nach draußen gebracht und mir Wasser gegeben, aber ich konnte die restliche Nacht nicht aufhören zu zittern. 		3 0 2 1 3 3 1 0
ptsd_147 eng I’m a trans woman. At the time of this experience, I had been living as myself for about three years and had started hormones two years before. I’d been struggling with anxiety and old family trauma, and I’d heard good things about ayahuasca from a friend. I found a retreat online that described itself as ‘inclusive and heart-centred’. On the application form I wrote that I was trans. Nobody said anything about it.

When I arrived, the shaman, an older man from another country, seemed friendly. The facilitators were a European couple who translated for him. On the first evening there was a group circle where we introduced ourselves. When it was my turn, I said my name and that I’m a trans woman. The shaman said something to the facilitators, and they hesitated before translating. Eventually the woman said that the shaman ‘honoured my journey’ and that the medicine would ‘help me find balance in my energies’. I felt a little uneasy but let it go.

The first ceremony was fine, mostly physical, a lot of purging. In the second ceremony, the shaman came to sit in front of me to do a ‘healing’. He blew tobacco smoke over me and sang. Then he started speaking, and the male facilitator translated in a low voice. He said that he saw a ‘masculine spirit trapped and suffering’ inside me, and that he would help free it. He said the ‘confusion’ I was in was caused by a dark energy that had entered me in childhood. He pressed his hand hard on my chest, where my breasts are, and said he was ‘removing the false feminine’.

I was deep in the medicine. I couldn’t speak. I couldn’t move. I wanted to scream at him to stop, but it was like my body belonged to someone else. And worse, part of me, in that state, started to believe him. I saw images of myself as a boy, the boy I was forced to be for so long, crying in a dark room. I saw my father’s face, telling me to ‘man up’. I felt that everything I had built, my name, my body, my life, was a lie and that I was being punished for it. I felt my identity crumbling, and I didn’t know who I was anymore. Not a woman, not a man, just a shattered thing on the floor.

He went on singing for what felt like hours. At one point he called me by my old name, the name I haven’t used in years, which I had never told anyone at the retreat. I still don’t know how he knew it, maybe it was in my passport, which they had copied for registration. Hearing it in that state was like being thrown back into my childhood bedroom.

When the ceremony ended, I crawled to my bed and lay there shaking until morning. At breakfast the female facilitator came to me and said that she understood it was a ‘challenging’ night, but that the shaman was ‘very powerful’ and saw things we couldn’t. She said that some people come to the medicine with ‘mental constructs’ that need to be released. I told her I wanted to leave. She said that leaving in the middle of the process could be dangerous for my spirit. I left anyway, that afternoon, with a taxi to the nearest town and a bus to the airport.

On the bus I kept touching my chest where his hand had been and feeling sick. 		3 3 3 2 2 3 3 0

ptsd_150 eng I’m a nervous flyer, and before a long-haul flight to visit family in Australia, a friend suggested I take a small dose of mushrooms to ‘relax’. It was the worst advice I’ve ever received. I ate them in the airport toilet before boarding.

About an hour after take-off, the plane started to feel like a metal tube full of strangers breathing my air. The engine noise became a scream. Every bump of turbulence was the plane falling apart. It was a terrible idea. The diaries were full of things I had forgotten or pushed away. Pages and pages about wanting to die. Lists of ways to do it. Descriptions of cutting myself. Entries addressed to my parents that I never gave them, saying I was sorry for being a burden. The handwriting was childish and shaky and in places the ink was smudged from tears.

On LSD, the words came off the page and filled the room. I wasn’t reading them anymore, I was inside them. I was 15 again, sitting on the floor of my old bedroom, with the same hopelessness, the same certainty that nobody would ever understand me. The years in between disappeared. My PhD, my friends, my partner, everything I’d built felt like a thin story I’d made up to cover the truth, which was that I was still that girl and always would be.

I started to feel the old pull. The thought came, very calm and clear, that I should finish what I hadn’t managed at 15. It didn’t feel like a choice, more like a fact. I couldn’t really talk. I just said ‘please come’. She came within half an hour and stayed with me until the next morning, holding my hand while I lay on the sofa, alternating between staring at the ceiling and sobbing. The words from the diaries kept crawling on the walls. 		3 1 2 1 0 2 2 1

ptsd_183 eng This happened when I was 26, and I’m 31 now. I’ll try to describe it as fully as I can, because I’ve only ever told pieces of it.

I was living in a shared house with four other people. One of my housemates, I’ll call her R, was into psychedelics and spirituality, and she was organising a ‘full moon ceremony’ in the garden with some friends from her meditation group. She invited me. There would be mushroom tea and a fire. I’d only done mushrooms once before, a small amount at a festival, and I liked it. I said yes.

There were about eight of us around the fire. R made the tea in a big pot and served it in mugs. I didn’t know how much was in each mug. In hindsight, I think the tea was very strong and the dosing very uneven. The first hour was lovely. We sang some songs R had taught us. The fire crackled. The moon came up over the neighbours’ roofs, enormous and orange.

Then, gradually, I noticed that I couldn’t follow the songs anymore. The words lost their meaning. The faces around the fire started to look like masks, flickering in the firelight, and behind each mask I sensed something else, something not human. The fire became a mouth. The moon became an eye. I felt a huge, cold attention focus on me, the same way you might focus on an insect.

I tried to say something to R, but my voice sounded wrong, deep and slow, like a recording played at the wrong speed. She smiled at me and said ‘let it come’. I don’t think she realised how bad it was. I started to lose the sense of where my body ended. My hands were part of the grass. My breathing was the wind. I felt myself spreading out over the garden, thinner and thinner, until there was hardly anything left. And then there was a moment, I can’t say how long, when there was nothing at all. No me, no garden, no moon. Just a black, silent, infinite absence.

When I came back from that, I was in total panic. I didn’t know who I was or what I was. I knew there had been a ‘before’, but I couldn’t remember it. I had a body but didn’t know how to use it. I tried to stand and fell into the flower bed. Someone helped me up and I screamed at them, because their face was a mask with nothing behind it.

I ran into the house. Inside, under the electric light, everything was even worse. The kitchen looked like a hospital, sterile and threatening. The fridge was humming a threatening note. I went to my room and locked the door. I sat on my bed and tried to remember my name. I found my wallet and looked at my ID card. The name meant nothing. The face in the photo meant nothing. I remember looking at it and thinking: this is a stranger, and I’ve stolen his life.

I don’t know how long I sat there. At some point R knocked and asked if I was okay. I didn’t answer. She went away. Later, another housemate who hadn’t taken anything, I’ll call him T, knocked and said he was worried, and asked if he could come in. I opened the door because his voice sounded normal. He sat with me on the floor. He didn’t try to explain anything. He just talked about ordinary things: the football results, a film he’d seen, what he was going to cook tomorrow. I didn’t understand most of it, but the ordinariness was like a rope. He stayed with me until it was light.

When the sun came up I knew my name again. But the feeling that it was someone else’s name, that I was living in a stolen life, didn’t go away with the drug. That feeling has been with me, on and off, ever since.

The next day R came to my room with a cup of tea and said it sounded like I’d had a ‘beautiful ego death’. I asked her to leave. I moved out two months later. 		3 3 3 3 1 3 3 0

ptsd_191 eng I’ll try to tell this in order, because it’s the only way I can make sense of it.

I’m a nurse, and three years ago I was at the end of a very bad year. My mother had died, my long relationship had ended, and work in the ICU during the last Covid wave had left me exhausted and numb. A colleague, also a nurse, told me about ayahuasca and how it had helped her process her grief. She gave me the contact of a group that met in a farmhouse a couple of hours from where I live. The first ceremony was hard but meaningful. I cried a lot about my mother, and at one point I felt her presence, warm and kind. I purged several times. I felt cleaner afterwards and I was glad I’d come.

The second night was different. The leader, a man in his sixties, said that the second night is when the medicine ‘goes deeper’, and he served a larger cup. About an hour after drinking, I started to see the ICU. Not as a memory, but as if I were there. The beeping of the monitors, the hiss of the ventilators, the smell of disinfectant. I saw the faces of patients I’d lost, one after another. There had been many. I’d never allowed myself to count them. In the vision they were lying in rows, and each one turned their head to look at me.

Then I saw my mother among them, in a hospital bed, on a ventilator. She had actually died at home, of cancer, not in an ICU. But in the vision she was there, and her eyes were open and terrified, and she was trying to say something and couldn’t because of the tube. I was her nurse. I was supposed to help her. And I couldn’t move. I stood there in my scrubs and watched the monitor flatline.

I started screaming. I was sure I was actually there. One of the helpers came and put his hand on my back and said something like ‘you’re safe, it’s the medicine’. I couldn’t hear it. His hand felt like a patient’s hand, cold. I tore away from him and crawled across the floor to a corner.

After that, things fragmented. I lost any sense of being a person. I was the ICU. I was every alarm going off at once. I was the guilt of every death. I felt that I was being judged by all of the dead, and that the verdict was that I should join them. I remember thinking very clearly that the only way to make it stop was to die, and I started looking for a way out of the room. I think I tried to get to the door. Someone held me back. I fought them. I bit someone’s arm, I found out later.

They had to hold me down, three of them. The leader came and sang over me and blew tobacco smoke in my face, which made me choke and feel like I was suffocating, like the patients who couldn’t breathe. I could feel my lungs filling with fluid.

It lasted, I’m told, about four hours. When it finally began to ease, I was lying on a mattress in the corner, soaked in sweat and vomit, shaking. Someone had put a blanket over me. I didn’t know who I was or where I was for a long time. The first thing I recognised was the smell of the woodstove, and I held on to it like a rope.

In the morning the leader told me that I had ‘released a lot of collective trauma’ and that I was a ‘healer’, and that this was my initiation. The person I had bitten had a bruise on his arm and was very kind about it. I couldn’t look at anyone. I drove home, which I shouldn’t have done, and I don’t remember most of the drive. 		3 3 3 3 3 3 3 0

ptsd_195 eng I’d been taking psychedelics for about ten years and considered myself experienced. I’d read all the books, done many trips, some difficult, and always come through. In hindsight, that confidence was dangerous.

I wanted to do what some people call a ‘heroic’ LSD trip: a very high dose, alone, in nature, with no music and no distractions. I rented a remote cabin in the mountains for a week in January. It had a woodstove and no phone signal. I told a friend where I was and that I’d call him when I got back to the village on the fifth day. I took about 1000ug on the second morning.

For the first hours it was overwhelming but also magnificent. The snow was glowing, the mountains were breathing, I felt that I was seeing the structure of the universe. I stood outside in the snow for a long time, barefoot I think, though I didn’t notice the cold. I felt that I was the mountain, the snow, the sky, all at once.

At some point I lost the thread completely. There was no more ‘I’ who was seeing the mountain. There were no more mountains. There was a vast, white, silent field, and nothing in it. I don’t know how long I was there. Hours, maybe. When something like a self came back, it didn’t know what it was. I didn’t know I was a human being. I had a body, but I didn’t know what it was for. I didn’t know what the cabin was, or what cold was, or what I was supposed to do.

The next thing I remember with any clarity is being inside the cabin, lying on the floor, and it was dark. The fire in the woodstove had gone out. I was shaking violently. My feet hurt in a strange, burning way and I couldn’t feel my toes. I still didn’t really know who I was, but my body knew that it was in danger. I crawled to the stove and tried to light it, but my hands didn’t work properly. I couldn’t figure out the matches. They kept turning into insects in my hand. It took me what felt like an hour to get a fire going.

Then the second wave hit, or maybe it was the cold and exhaustion. I spent the night in a kind of delirium, half on LSD, half in hypothermia. I saw figures in the corners of the cabin, tall and thin, standing silently. I talked to them. I asked them if I was dead. They didn’t answer. At times I was sure that I had died out in the snow and that this cabin was some kind of waiting room. At other times I was sure I’d been in the cabin for years and would never leave.

When daylight came, I was still disoriented, but I knew my name again. My feet were swollen and blistered and some of my toes were white. I understood that I had frostbite. I couldn’t walk to the village on those feet, it was eight kilometres. I spent two more days in the cabin, keeping the fire going, eating crackers, and trying to stay sane. I had no idea if my toes would have to be amputated. The LSD had worn off, but I was in a strange state, very fragile, with flashes of the white field whenever I closed my eyes.

On the fifth day, when I didn’t call, my friend called the mountain rescue. They came on a snowmobile and found me. I spent a week in hospital. I lost the tips of two toes. 		3 3 3 2 3 3 1 0

ptsd_200 eng This is about the night my son was born. I’m still not sure how to talk about it.

My wife was 36 weeks pregnant. Her due date was a month away, and we’d agreed that I would have one last ‘free’ weekend with my best friends before the baby. We went to a cabin about three hours away, and on the Saturday evening we took LSD. My wife knew I was going and what I was planning. I will never forget the feeling of that moment. Everything in the room seemed to fall apart. I couldn’t understand what she was saying at first. Her voice was coming through in waves of colour. One of my friends called a taxi from the nearest town. It took an hour to arrive. During that hour I was walking in circles around the cabin, crying, calling my wife over and over. ptsd_205 eng I want to write this out fully, because the short version, ‘I had a bad trip and ended up in a psychiatric hospital’, doesn’t capture what it was like, and because I think the details of how it went wrong could help someone.

Background: I was 24, working in a call centre, living with two flatmates. I’d had depression in my teens, but I’d been okay for a couple of years. I’d taken mushrooms twice and LSD once, all small doses, all positive. My flatmate K had just come back from a festival with some LSD tabs and said they were ‘quite strong, maybe split one’. I didn’t split it. I took the whole tab on a Saturday afternoon. K took half, and our other flatmate didn’t take anything but was home.

The first two hours: the come-up was faster and stronger than anything I’d felt before. Within forty minutes the carpet was rippling and the walls were covered in patterns. That part was fun. We put on music and lay on the floor. K was laughing a lot. I remember feeling very happy and close to her.

The turn: around the two-hour mark, I went to the bathroom. I looked in the mirror and my pupils were enormous, black holes. I stared into them and felt like I was falling in. Behind my eyes there was a corridor, and at the end of the corridor something was waiting. I knew I shouldn’t look, but I couldn’t stop. When I finally pulled away from the mirror, I felt that something had followed me out. A presence behind my left shoulder. I turned around and nothing was there, but the feeling stayed.

I went back to the living room and tried to tell K. She said ‘it’s just the acid’ and turned the music up. The music had changed. It was something with a heavy bass, and every beat felt like a footstep coming closer. The presence was still behind me. I started glancing over my shoulder every few seconds. K thought it was funny at first, then she stopped laughing.

The fragmentation: the next part is hard to describe in order, because it wasn’t in order. I remember the living room lights getting brighter and brighter until everything was white. I remember being in the kitchen with a glass of water and not knowing what water was for. I remember sitting on the floor of my bedroom, holding my knees, rocking. I remember hearing a voice, very clearly, saying my name and then ‘it’s over now’. I took that to mean my life was over. I remember lying on my bed and feeling my body sinking into it, through it, into the floor, into the building, into the earth, until there was no body and no me, just a heavy, dark pressure and a voice repeating ‘it’s over now’.

The flatmates: our sober flatmate, J, came into my room at some point. He told me later that I was lying on the bed with my eyes open, not responding, and that when he touched my arm I screamed and backed into the corner. He said I kept saying ‘it’s over, it’s over, I’m already dead’. He tried to talk to me for half an hour. I didn’t recognise him. I thought he was the thing from behind the mirror, wearing J’s face. K was in her own room, crying, too scared to come in.

The ambulance: J called an ambulance after about an hour of trying to calm me down, because I had started hitting my head against the wall. Two paramedics came, a man and a woman. The woman was very calm and kind. She crouched down and talked to me in a quiet voice. I remember her saying ‘you’ve taken something, it’s making you feel this way, it will wear off’. For a moment that made sense, like a door opening. Then the door closed again and I was sure she was lying, that this was how they took you to the place where the dead go.

The hospital: in A&E they gave me a sedative. I remember the needle and a very cold feeling spreading up my arm. I slept, or something like sleep. When I woke up it was night and I was on a trolley in a corridor, and I didn’t know how much time had passed. The LSD was still working, but more weakly, and the sedative had made everything heavy and muddy. A doctor came and asked me questions. I couldn’t answer most of them. I told her I thought I had died. She wrote something down.

Because I couldn’t say clearly that I wasn’t going to hurt myself, and because of the head-banging, they admitted me to the psychiatric ward for observation. I was there for four days. The first two days I was still not right. The presence behind my shoulder was still there. Every door slamming made me jump. The other patients scared me, though they were mostly just as frightened as I was. I didn’t sleep much. I was ashamed and terrified that I’d broken my mind forever.

ptsd_217 eng I was 30 and had been in a stable relationship for five years. My partner and I decided to try MDMA and then mushrooms together at home, as a kind of relationship-deepening experience, after reading about couples doing this. The MDMA part was lovely, we talked about our feelings and felt very close. When the mushrooms kicked in, about two hours later, things changed.

I started seeing my partner as a stranger. Not in a paranoid way at first, more like I was seeing her clearly for the first time, and she was someone I didn’t know at all. Then I started remembering every small hurt between us, every time she’d dismissed me, every argument, every disappointment, and they piled up into a mountain. I felt that I’d been lying to myself for five years and that our relationship was empty.

I told her this. I said things I’d never said before, cruel things, and at the time they felt like the truth. She started crying. She said things back. Her face kept changing, sometimes it was her, sometimes it was my mother, sometimes it was a skull. I felt that I was drowning in a flood of resentment that had been waiting for this moment.

Then I started to dissolve. I didn’t know if I was the one speaking or if the words were coming through me from somewhere else. I felt that I had no self, just a collection of old injuries. I lay on the floor and couldn’t move for a long time. She sat on the sofa crying, and we didn’t touch for hours.

In the morning we were both exhausted and raw. We didn’t know how to go back to normal. We broke up three months later. I still don’t know if the mushrooms showed us something true, or if they created a truth that hadn’t been there before. 		3 2 2 1 0 2 3 0
