Qualitative examples.

Illustrative examples for the responses that most reduced the residuals are presented in Table 5. This table reports on the model that only contains the "mental health"-responses, as only these add predictive accuracy descriptively (see above; the increase is not reliable, so these examples should be read with particular caution). In a qualitative interpretation, it is striking that strong negative prediction shifts are often associated to responses that describe indifference -here, it seems that the regression model based on the other predictors otherwise overshoots in its predictions of well-being. Beyond that, other responses associated to strong negative shifts describe (too) short-lived effects, or no impact of the experience (here, the model predictions based on the other predictors appear to otherwise overshoot). Strong positive shifts on the other hand are often associated to responses describing euphoria, connectedness and love, open-mindedness, and newly-found appreciation of life.

PTSD

Quantitative analysis.

For the main outcome PCL (PTSD symptom severity), the cross-validated R² values of the different elastic net models in the nested hierarchy (baseline models, extended-by-text models, as well as the text-only model) are presented in Table 6. The text-only model on its own (with information from all three responses) already achieves a relatively high R² = .230. In the pre-specified test of the extended-by-text model including all three free-text responses, we observe a ∆R² = .097 from R² = .308 in the baseline model to R² = .405 (95% CI [.038, .157], t(99) = 3.26, p = .002) -an absolute increase of 9.7% and a relative increase of 31.6%. In the setup where text data is the most helpful in addition to the other predictors, the extended-by-text model including the post and treat free-text responses, we observe a ∆R² = .110 to R² = .418 (95% CI [.050, .171], p < .001, not corrected for the selection of this model among the seven extended-by-text models).

As can be seen in Table 6, the increase is carried primarily by the "post" and secondarily by the "treat" responses: The models including only one of them achieve ∆R² = .088 (post) and ∆R² = .056 (treat), which are both reliable on their own, while the "acute" responses do not add predictive accuracy (∆R² = -.003).

For the additional outcome PTGI (post-traumatic growth), text data does not add to the variance explained. The baseline model achieves R² = .355; the pre-specified extended-by-text model with all three responses reaches R² = .339 (∆R² = -.016, 95% CI [-.057, .025], p = .446). In fact, all seven extended-by-text models slightly decrease the R² compared to the baseline model (which is possible with held-out R² ); even the best-performing one (using the treat responses only) reaches R² = .353 (∆R² = -.002, p = .918). The text-only model only reaches R² = .035 (in 32 of the outer folds, this model shrank all text coefficients to zero and predicted a constant value, so that no R² could be computed; these folds are not included in the average). As in the APEQ and GCMQ data, the overlap between the free-text data and the other predictors is small to moderate (Table 2).

Qualitative examples.

Illustrative examples for the responses that most reduced the residuals are presented in Table 7. This table reports on the model that only contains the "post"-responses, as these are the single response with the largest increase in R² .

In a qualitative interpretation, free-text responses with very positive shift values (i.e., increases in symptom severity) for the most part simply describe (severe) symptoms of mental disorders across the board, and not restricted to PTSD symptoms. It may not be too surprising that this information helps predicting PTSD symptom severity. Free-text responses with very negative shift values (i.e., decreases in symptom severity) mostly state that there were no persistent difficulties, or describe insights about oneself.

Discussion

Free-text responses are frequently collected in clinical studies, but are often not analyzed systematically and rigorously. In the present study, we investigated to what extent the information in participant's free-text responses can be harvested with text embedding models to increase the held-out predictive accuracy for relevant outcome measures above and beyond sizable collections of standard predictors (see Figure 1).

Specifically, we investigated free-text responses describing experiences associated with psychedelic substance use, in addition to demographic predictors, setting variables, and series of questionnaire scores.

Discussion of current findings

Across three large datasets (Evens et al., 2026; Wolff et al., 2022 Wolff et al., , 2024) ) with five different outcome measures, the increase in predictive accuracy is sometimes substantial (Table 1): We find significant increases in predictive accuracy between around 3% and 10% for predicting changes in subjective well-being (APEQ WHO-5), changes in psychological flexibility (APEQ AAQ-II) and post-traumatic stress disorder symptom severity (PTSD PCL-5).

As the variances explained range around 30% to 40%, these increases matter.

However, such result patterns are not ubiquitous: For well-being (GCMQ WEMWBS) and post-traumatic growth (PTSD PTGI), we find no significant increases. These results replicate in a robustness check with a second text embedding model (bge-m3 ; see the Supplementary Material). As can be seen in Table 2, overlap between text embeddings and other predictors is generally small to moderate. The free-text responses thus contain information not captured by the other measurement tools. Qualitative inspections suggest that the most predictive free-text responses contain a broad range of relatively straightforward information: emotional reactions, indifference, meta-cognitive processes, or symptoms of mental disorders. Notably, in our reading the predictive texts mainly convey psychological information on the participant's own cognitive and emotional states, rather than information about the outside world (such as events or settings).

Concerning the GCMQ results, it may be initially tempting to attribute the lower ∆R² to the much larger number of other predictors considered in the analysis (which stems from the fact that more such predictors are available in the dataset). However, in Table 1 one can clearly see that the ∆R² values in the model comparisons are very much aligned with the R² values of the text-only models. Sample size is also not the determinant of these findings -the sample size of the PTSD-PCL-5 data is below half of the GCMQ data, but the ∆R² is much higher. And within the PTSD data, ∆R² differs substantially between the two different outcomes PCL-5 and PTGI, even though the set of baseline predictors is identical. This indicates that in cases like the GCMQ data (or the PTSD-PTGI data), the text genuinely carries less information about the outcomes.

One potential reason for the discrepancy between the APEQ-WHO-5 and the GCMQ(-WEMWBS) results, where both outcome variables are well-being measures, may be the different nature of the free-text responses: In the GCMQ data, participants do not describe the experience itself, but its perceived impact on stress handling and mental health. However, there are also other differences: WEMWBS in the GCMQ data is a state-level variable of current well-being, while WHO-5 in the APEQ data is a retrospective assessment of the difference in well-being before and after the psychedelic experience. Also R² is generally lower for all models in the GCMQ data than in the APEQ data (which may be a consequence of the different types of outcome variables, as most baseline predictors of the APEQ models are also included in the GCMQ models, with the exception of duration, mood, preparedness, strength of the effects, and the APEQ-ACE ×

APEQ-AVE interaction).

In the PTSD-PTGI data, the most reasonable conclusion to us is that the free-text responses just do not carry information about posttraumatic growth, in particular because the questions focused on symptoms. As the question did not ask for posttraumatic growth, and many participants may not have experienced this or may not even be aware of the concept, findings such as these are bound to occur -as any other variable, free-text responses will not be a universal predictor of every possible outcome. In addition, the concept and its measurement itself have received criticism in the literature Frazier et al., 2009; Jayawickreme et al., 2021, which may lead to difficulties in predicting this variable.

The role of open-ended free-text responses

Of course, analyses of free-text responses are and have been performed already (Mayring, 2014), often requiring highly effortful and resource-intensive human annotation Braun and Clarke, 2006; O'Connor and Joffe, 2020. As a direct consequence, there are serious issues with scalability to large datasetsfoot_2 . In contrast, applying techniques from machine learning/NLP is often just a matter of seconds or maybe minutes. Such techniques have been available for some time, for example using word counts (Tausczik & Pennebaker, 2010), but also vector representation models such as Latent Semantic Analysis or word2vec have already been used to analyze free-text responses also in clinical settings Barattieri di San Pietro et al., 2023; De Boer et al., 2018; Elvevåg et al., 2007; Kintsch, 2002. With context-aware text embeddings models, where texts are no longer treated as an unordered bag of words, this vector space approach has become far more sophisticated and powerful. Text embeddings do not annotate a set of defined criteria, but instead are general-level quantitative representations of the text and its meaning. This has the disadvantage that these embeddings are not directly interpretable, but the advantage that they encode whatever the participant produced without requiring a top-down filter of search criteria.

Concerning the disadvantage of initial non-interpretability, this is one that can be addressed. Common approaches cluster analyses on text embeddings that allow researchers to assess common themes and topics (Grootendorst, 2022; Lalk et al., 2024), or regression-based approaches to predict pre-defined semantic dimensions such as valence from text embeddings (Gatti et al., 2024). In the present study, our approach to establish interpretability was to examine the responses that contributed the most to making the predictions more accurate (i.e., decreased residuals the most). As showcased in the Results sections, this reveals valuable information provided by participants, and common themes in their responses.

This ties in to a more general point about free-text responses: In standard questionnaire items the researcher has to determine which construct they aim to measure (and ideally then evaluate the item), and the item then serves as a "fishing net" to catch exactly that construct. Open-ended free-text responses function fundamentally different as they are inherently personalized: Depending on how open the questions are worded, participants are completely free to produce whatever they themselves deem relevant or informative. The selection is thus passed from researcher to participant. In the words of Schwartz et al. (2013), "the data itself drives a comprehensive exploration of language that distinguishes people, finding connections that are not captured with traditional closed-vocabulary word-category analyses" (see also Boyd and Schwartz, 2021).

This opens up a very simple opportunity to catch information we might otherwise have missed, because (to stay in the metaphor), the meshes of the fishing net were too large, or the net was in a wrong place entirely. We do not want to claim that no questionnaire items can be developed to catch this information -this possibility surely exists (the net can be changed or moved). In our qualitative examinations of what responses increase predictive accuracy, the relevant dimensions appear to be rather obvious, for example describing evaluations, meta-cognitive processes, or symptoms of mental disorders. Still, even though seemingly similar items existed in the questionnaires (for example, about the valence and retrospective appraisal of the psychedelic experience), these apparently did not capture the relevant information. This demonstrates that open-ended free-text responses can always function as a convenient back-up to capture information that could otherwise be missed. This is especially relevant in data collection scenarios where one cannot or does not want to let the participants fill in questionnaires for hours. As argued by (Kjell et al., 2019 (Kjell et al., , 2022)), participants also often perceive the free-text response format as more natural than standard questionnaire items which force them to translate some subjective experience into a single number. Open-ended questions with free-text responses may also address issues with suggestive questions in research surveys.

In research on psychedelic experiences, there is currently a debate that standard questionnaire items can push participants to focus on specific dimensions of their experience and reinforce stereotypical perspectives, which can bias the data (Vanderijst et al., 2026). Open-ended questions can be formulated very generically ("Describe your psychedelic experience"), so that such biases can be largely avoided.

Practical recommendation

Based on our study, our practical recommendation is to include at least one open-ended question with a free-text response format into any questionnaire. Even if it just "Is there anything else you want to tell us?" with an obligatory response field that requires a minimal amount of characters, there may always be useful information that would otherwise be missed. Text embeddings -from open, locally-run models to ensure data protection -make it very convenient to analyze such responses, so researchers do not have to worry about time-and resource-intensive annotation steps. The analysis pipeline presented in the present article can serve as a template for this (see also Debelak et al., 2025; Kjell et al., 2023). Similar methods can, and have been, applied for clinical diagnoses -for example, researchers have used patients' free-text data from interviews of spontaneous speech as the input for classifiers trained to perform clinical diagnoses (Agbavor & Liang, 2022; F. Chen et al., 2025 F. Chen et al., , 2026)).

Of course, if more specific questions are included -such as the questions to describe the psychedelic experiences in our current study -this can only add more information.

Depending on the research question and the data collection setting, this introduces a tradeoff question between time and resources invested and informative data points collected. As the human communicative system has developed under evolutionary pressure to efficiently convey rich information (Gibson et al., 2019), we suspect that this tradeoff may often play out in favor of open-ended free-text responses.

Data availability

The full reproducible analysis pipeline for all analyses presented here is available in a Zenodo repository at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24303102. Since the data contains sensitive private information, the original data cannot be made publicly available. The reproducible pipeline thus runs all analyses with synthetic data created to resemble the original data. Manuscript versions created from this synthetic data, with all changes from the present manuscript marked, are available at the Zenodo repository.

AI usage statement

The first version of the analysis pipeline was implemented manually in R. AI tools (Claude Code; Sonnet and Opus, versions 5 and 5.5) were used on toy data to streamline and better structure the scripts, to adapt the script for all datasets and outcome variables, to create a structured and reproducible repository that flows into a reproducible L A T E Xdocument, and for literature search. No AI tools were used for writing the first complete version of the manuscript text; AI tools were then used to implement selected changes to the methods and analysis after internal revisions, and draft the corresponding suggestions for changes to Methods and Results. All AI-suggested modifications were manually reviewed and validated by the first author.

Supplementary Material: Hyperparameter sweep and bge-m3 model

Figure 2 presents the cross-validated R² for all elastic net models reported in the main paper for different numbers of PCA components of the multilingual-e5-large embeddings that are entered as predictors. These results are based on a single (non-repeated, non-nested) 10-fold cross-validation run, as repeating the nested cross-validation for every number of components would have been computationally prohibitive. As the hyperparameters are selected on the same folds that are used for evaluation here, these R² values tend to be optimistic compared to the nested results in the main text (hardly in the APEQ data, but more clearly in the GCMQ data and especially in the comparatively small PTSD dataset); the informative part is therefore the comparison across numbers of components. In the APEQ and GCMQ data, R² increases steeply up to about 10-15 components and remains largely stable up to about 40 components before slowly decreasing; the 20 components used in the main analysis lie within this stable range. For PCL-5 in the PTSD data, the pattern is similar but noisier.

For PTGI, no number of components leads to an increase over the baseline model. Figure 3 presents the same information for the bge-m3 embeddings, where we find comparable results, with one exception: for PCL-5, R² continues to increase up to 40-60 components, so that the main analysis with 20 components is, if anything, conservative here (although the gains at larger numbers of components, estimated on fewer than 210 training participants, are particularly prone to the optimism described above). These results for the bge-m3 analysis are summarized in Table 8, in the same format as Table 1 for the main multilingual-e5-large analysis.

Figure 1.

To assess the added predictive accuracy brought about by free-text data, we estimated nested regression models for each outcome variable: The main analysis relies on a baseline model containing what has been defined in the Method sections as "other predictor variables" (the upper, blue track of Figure1), and "extended-by-text" models that additionally include the 20 text-embedding principal components for a specific free-text response (the rightmost, purple part of Figure1, combining the blue and orange tracks).

it is also evident that information encoded in the text data (a) goes far beyond what these questionnaires measure, and (b) this additional information is useful for predicting differences in the outcome variables.

For

differences in psychological flexibility (AAQ-II), the most-improving responses are presented in Table 4. Note again that positive changes indicate a decrease in flexibility, while negative changes indicate an increase in flexibility. The pattern here is thus in line with what we observe for the WHO-5 prediction: Reports of self-awareness, re-evaluation, and meta-cognition are associated to more positive changes (= decreases) in psychological flexibility, while reports of content, serenity, and happiness are associated to more negative changes (= increases).

The very points discussed so far also come with limitations: Since participants choose what responses they provide and what type of information they present in their responses, there is very little researcher control. For instance, even a single participant response will likely often not focus on a single construct or concept, but touch on different, possibly only loosely related or unrelated concepts. The same will likely apply for responses collected from different participants, who may choose to focus on entirely different aspects of a topic or even entirely different topics. Depending on the research question and objective, this may introduce unacceptable noise to the study. Additionally, open-ended response by their nature often prevent the researcher from cleanly pre-defining the construct or concept they are supposed to measure. This makes them a risky or often unusable choice for confirmatory hypothesis-testing, where a specific relation between specific variables is at the center of the research question.
